questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven characteristics of living things?
questions.explanation: The recognised characteristics of life are nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth, reproduction, irritability, and movement; crystallization is a physical, non-living process.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms is the
questions.explanation: The cell theory establishes the cell as the smallest unit capable of carrying out all life processes independently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which organelle is described as the 'powerhouse of the cell' because it is the site of aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria contain the enzymes for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, generating most of a cell's ATP through aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall external to the cell membrane, providing shape and support, which animal cells lack.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The correct order of increasing complexity in the organization of living matter is
questions.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together as systems, representing increasing levels of biological organization.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which kingdom includes organisms that are prokaryotic, unicellular, and lack a true nucleus?
questions.explanation: Kingdom Monera comprises bacteria and cyanobacteria, whose cells are prokaryotic, lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and other organelles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Fungi differ from green plants mainly in that fungi
options: have cell walls made of cellulose
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophic, absorbing nutrients from organic matter, since they lack chlorophyll and the chloroplasts needed for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The chloroplast, found in green plant cells, is the site of
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll pigments that trap light energy, driving the photosynthetic conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which cell organelle controls the cell's activities and contains the hereditary material?
questions.explanation: The nucleus houses the chromosomes (DNA), directing protein synthesis and cellular activity, and is often called the control centre of the cell.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Binomial nomenclature, the scientific naming system for organisms, was introduced by
questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus developed the two-name (genus and species) system of naming organisms, still used in modern taxonomy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which taxonomic rank groups together organisms of similar genera?
questions.explanation: Taxonomic hierarchy from broadest to narrowest is Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species; a family groups related genera.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The cell membrane's main function is to
options: regulate the movement of substances into and out of the cell
questions.explanation: The selectively permeable cell membrane controls which substances enter or leave the cell, maintaining internal homeostasis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best defines a tissue?
options: A group of different organs working together
A group of similar cells performing a specific function
A single cell performing all life functions
The outer covering of an organism
questions.explanation: A tissue is an organized group of structurally similar cells that work together to carry out one or more specific functions, such as muscle tissue contracting.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Ribosomes in a cell are mainly responsible for
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA into polypeptide chains, making them the site of protein synthesis in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a dicotyledonous root, the region responsible for absorbing water and mineral salts is the
questions.explanation: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area of the epidermis in the root hair (piliferous) zone, maximising water and mineral ion absorption.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The main function of the xylem tissue in a flowering plant is to
options: conduct manufactured food from the leaves to other parts
conduct water and dissolved mineral salts upward from the root
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are dead, lignified tubes that transport water and dissolved minerals from roots to the rest of the plant, and also provide structural support.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Phloem tissue is primarily responsible for
options: translocation of manufactured food (mainly sucrose) from the leaves to other parts
absorption of water from the soil
transport of water from roots to leaves
questions.explanation: Phloem, composed of living sieve tubes and companion cells, translocates organic food substances made in the leaves to storage organs and growing regions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which mammalian organ system is responsible for pumping blood around the body?
questions.explanation: The heart, the central pumping organ of the circulatory system, rhythmically contracts to propel blood through arteries, capillaries, and veins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Photosynthesis in green plants requires which combination of raw materials?
questions.explanation: The overall equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, requiring carbon dioxide and water as raw materials.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Heterotrophic nutrition in which an organism lives in or on another living organism, deriving nutrients and causing it harm, is called
questions.explanation: Parasitic nutrition involves an organism (the parasite) obtaining nutrients from a living host, usually to the host's detriment, e.g., tapeworms in the human gut.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Saprophytic nutrition involves an organism obtaining nutrients by
options: manufacturing its own food using light energy
living inside a host and absorbing digested food directly
ingesting solid food and digesting it internally
secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the digested products
questions.explanation: Saprophytes such as many fungi and bacteria carry out extracellular digestion, releasing enzymes onto dead matter and absorbing the soluble products.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The mammalian tooth adapted for cutting and biting off food is the
questions.explanation: Incisors are chisel-shaped teeth at the front of the jaw, adapted for cutting and biting food into manageable pieces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Canine teeth in carnivorous mammals are mainly adapted for
questions.explanation: Canines are pointed, conical teeth well adapted for piercing, gripping, and tearing flesh, especially prominent in carnivores.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which enzyme, present in saliva, begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase hydrolyses starch into maltose, beginning carbohydrate digestion even before food reaches the stomach.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Pepsin, a protein-digesting enzyme, is secreted in the
questions.explanation: Pepsin is secreted by gastric glands in the stomach and works optimally in the highly acidic environment created by hydrochloric acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood away from the heart to the rest of the body?
questions.explanation: The aorta is the largest artery, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle of the heart to systemic circulation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are mainly responsible for
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin within red blood cells binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it to respiring tissues throughout the body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which type of blood vessel has walls only one cell thick, allowing exchange of substances with tissues?
questions.explanation: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, with walls a single cell thick, permitting efficient diffusion of gases, nutrients, and wastes with surrounding tissues.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Aerobic respiration differs from anaerobic respiration mainly in that aerobic respiration
options: requires oxygen and releases far more energy per glucose molecule
produces lactic acid as the main end-product in animals
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose using oxygen, yielding about 38 ATP molecules, far more than the 2 ATP from anaerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, anaerobic respiration in muscles during vigorous exercise produces
questions.explanation: When oxygen supply is insufficient during strenuous activity, muscle cells respire anaerobically, converting glucose to lactic acid and releasing a small amount of energy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The main respiratory organ in fish, adapted for extracting dissolved oxygen from water, is the
questions.explanation: Fish gills have thin, highly vascularised filaments with a large surface area, adapted to extract dissolved oxygen efficiently from water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The main excretory product removed by the mammalian kidney is
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter blood and excrete urea, the main nitrogenous waste product formed from the breakdown of excess amino acids in the liver.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which excretory structure is found in earthworms, functioning similarly to the vertebrate kidney?
questions.explanation: Nephridia are the excretory organs of earthworms and other annelids, filtering coelomic fluid and expelling nitrogenous waste.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Malpighian tubules, the excretory organs of insects, empty their waste products into the
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules extract nitrogenous waste from the haemolymph and discharge it into the gut, where it is eliminated with faeces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The skin contributes to excretion mainly by removing excess
options: water, salts, and urea in sweat
questions.explanation: Sweat glands in the skin excrete water, dissolved salts, and small amounts of urea, also contributing to body temperature regulation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which tissue provides mechanical support in the stems of herbaceous (non-woody) plants?
questions.explanation: Collenchyma cells have unevenly thickened cellulose walls, providing flexible mechanical support especially in young, growing stems.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: An exoskeleton, as found in insects and crustaceans, is mainly composed of
questions.explanation: The insect exoskeleton (cuticle) is composed mainly of chitin, a tough polysaccharide that provides protection and attachment points for muscles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which type of joint permits movement in almost all directions, as found at the shoulder?
questions.explanation: A ball-and-socket joint, where a rounded bone head fits into a cup-like socket, allows the widest range of movement, as at the shoulder and hip.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A hinge joint, such as the elbow, permits movement
options: in one plane only, like a door hinge
questions.explanation: Hinge joints allow flexion and extension in a single plane, similar to the mechanical action of a door hinge, as seen at the elbow and knee.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The basic functional unit of the nervous system, responsible for transmitting nerve impulses, is the
questions.explanation: Neurons (nerve cells) are specialised to generate and conduct electrical impulses, forming the structural and functional basis of the nervous system.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The part of the human eye that controls the amount of light entering the eye by adjusting the size of the pupil is the
questions.explanation: The iris, a pigmented muscular diaphragm, contracts or relaxes to control pupil diameter and hence the amount of light reaching the retina.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Light-sensitive cells that detect the image formed in the eye are located in the
questions.explanation: The retina contains photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) that convert light into nerve impulses sent to the brain via the optic nerve.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which part of the mammalian ear is primarily responsible for maintaining balance?
questions.explanation: The three fluid-filled semicircular canals in the inner ear detect changes in the head's rotational movement, helping maintain balance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which endocrine gland, often called the 'master gland', regulates the activity of most other endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland secretes hormones that control the activity of other endocrine glands, including the thyroid, adrenal glands, and gonads.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Homeostasis is best defined as the
options: growth and development of an organism
maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes
process of obtaining food from the environment
questions.explanation: Homeostasis refers to the regulatory mechanisms that keep internal conditions such as temperature, water balance, and blood glucose within narrow, stable limits.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose levels after a meal is
questions.explanation: Insulin, secreted by the beta cells of the pancreas, stimulates cells to absorb glucose and promotes glycogen storage, lowering blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A deficiency in insulin production leads to a condition known as
questions.explanation: Without adequate insulin, cells cannot efficiently take up glucose, leading to persistently high blood glucose levels characteristic of diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The hormone glucagon, secreted by the pancreas, acts to
options: raise blood glucose levels by promoting the breakdown of glycogen to glucose
regulate water reabsorption in the kidney
lower blood glucose by promoting glycogen storage
questions.explanation: Glucagon opposes insulin, stimulating the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose when blood sugar levels fall too low.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Osmoregulation refers to the regulation of
options: water and salt balance in the body
questions.explanation: Osmoregulation maintains the correct concentration of water and dissolved solutes in body fluids, primarily controlled by the kidneys.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the kidney tubules, concentrating urine when the body is dehydrated?
questions.explanation: ADH, released by the pituitary gland, increases the permeability of the kidney's collecting ducts to water, reducing urine volume and conserving body water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Sweating helps regulate body temperature mainly by
options: evaporative cooling as sweat vaporises from the skin surface
trapping a layer of warm air near the skin
constricting blood vessels near the skin
increasing blood flow to the skin only
questions.explanation: As sweat evaporates from the skin, it absorbs latent heat from the body, producing a cooling effect that helps lower body temperature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Vasodilation of blood vessels near the skin surface in hot conditions helps the body to
options: lose more heat to the surroundings by increased blood flow near the surface
questions.explanation: When skin blood vessels widen (vasodilate), more warm blood flows near the skin surface, increasing heat loss to the environment by radiation and convection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Asexual reproduction in which a new individual develops as an outgrowth from the parent, as in Hydra, is called
questions.explanation: In budding, a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent and eventually detaches to become an independent organism, common in Hydra and yeast.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Binary fission, a form of asexual reproduction, is most typically seen in
questions.explanation: Binary fission involves a single-celled organism splitting into two genetically identical daughter cells, characteristic of bacteria and protozoans like Amoeba.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Vegetative propagation using stem cuttings, runners, or tubers is a form of
questions.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces new plants from vegetative parts (stems, roots, leaves) without the fusion of gametes, making it asexual.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In flowering plants, the male reproductive part of the flower is the
questions.explanation: The stamen, consisting of the anther and filament, produces pollen grains containing the male gametes of a flowering plant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or a different flower of the same species is called
questions.explanation: Pollination is the physical transfer of pollen to the stigma, a necessary precursor step before fertilisation (fusion of gametes) can occur.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Fertilisation in flowering plants occurs when
options: the male gamete nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus in the ovule
questions.explanation: After pollination, the pollen tube grows down to the ovule, delivering the male gamete nucleus, which fuses with the egg nucleus to form a zygote.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In mammals, fertilisation normally takes place in the
questions.explanation: The sperm typically meets and fertilises the egg in the oviduct, after which the resulting zygote travels to the uterus for implantation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The structure that connects the developing foetus to the uterine wall, allowing exchange of nutrients and waste, is the
questions.explanation: The placenta is a specialised organ that facilitates the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste products between the mother's blood and the foetus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of external fertilisation?
options: Fertilisation in most fish, where eggs and sperm are released into water
questions.explanation: In external fertilisation, gametes fuse outside the body, typically in water, as seen in most fish and amphibians, unlike the internal fertilisation in mammals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The amnion, a membrane surrounding the developing embryo in reptiles, birds, and mammals, functions mainly to
options: supply the embryo with food reserves
produce amniotic fluid that cushions and protects the embryo
anchor the embryo to the uterine wall
questions.explanation: The amnion secretes amniotic fluid, which cushions the embryo against mechanical shock and prevents desiccation, an adaptation for reproduction on land.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The hereditary material found in the nucleus of a cell, responsible for transmitting traits from parents to offspring, is
questions.explanation: DNA carries the genetic instructions encoded in genes, organized on chromosomes, and is passed from parents to offspring during reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A gene is best defined as
options: the physical appearance of an organism
a segment of DNA that codes for a particular trait or protein
questions.explanation: Genes are specific sequences of DNA located at particular positions (loci) on chromosomes, each typically coding for a specific protein or trait.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Alternative forms of a gene occupying the same position on homologous chromosomes are called
questions.explanation: Alleles are variant forms of the same gene (e.g., for flower colour) that occupy corresponding positions on a pair of homologous chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In Mendelian genetics, if a tall plant (Tt) is crossed with another tall plant (Tt), what proportion of the offspring is expected to be tall, assuming T is completely dominant over t?
questions.explanation: A Tt x Tt cross gives a genotype ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Since T is dominant, TT and Tt are both tall, giving 3/4 tall offspring by phenotype.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: An organism with two identical alleles for a given gene (e.g., TT or tt) is described as
questions.explanation: Homozygous describes an organism carrying two identical alleles for a particular gene, as opposed to heterozygous, which carries two different alleles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The observable physical or biochemical characteristics of an organism, resulting from its genotype and environment, is called its
questions.explanation: Phenotype refers to the outwardly expressed traits (e.g., flower colour, height) resulting from the interaction between an organism's genes and its environment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, red-green colour blindness is a sex-linked trait carried on the
questions.explanation: The gene for red-green colour blindness is located on the X chromosome, which explains why the condition is far more common in males (XY) than females (XX).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between a pure-breeding tall plant and a pure-breeding short plant, producing all tall offspring in the first generation, illustrates
questions.explanation: Mendel's principle of dominance states that in a heterozygote, one allele (the dominant one) masks the expression of the other (recessive) allele, giving uniform tall offspring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Continuous variation, such as human height, is characterised by
options: only a few sharply distinct categories, such as blood group
a gradual range of values with no distinct categories, usually influenced by many genes and the environment
being entirely unaffected by environmental factors
control by a single gene only
questions.explanation: Continuous variation, controlled by multiple genes (polygenic inheritance) and modified by environment, produces a smooth range of values rather than distinct classes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Discontinuous variation, such as human blood groups, is characterised by
options: being influenced mainly by environmental factors
distinct, separate categories with no intermediate forms
questions.explanation: Discontinuous variation produces clearly distinguishable categories (e.g., blood groups A, B, AB, O), typically controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The process by which chromosome number is halved during the formation of gametes is called
questions.explanation: Meiosis is a reduction division producing haploid gametes from diploid cells, ensuring the chromosome number is restored to diploid upon fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mitosis differs from meiosis in that mitosis produces
options: two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent
cells with half the chromosome number of the parent
questions.explanation: Mitosis is used for growth and repair, producing two diploid daughter cells identical to the parent cell, unlike meiosis, which halves the chromosome number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A test cross is used to determine
options: the exact phenotype of an organism
the number of chromosomes in a cell
whether an organism showing a dominant trait is homozygous or heterozygous
questions.explanation: Crossing an organism of unknown genotype (showing the dominant phenotype) with a homozygous recessive individual reveals, from the offspring ratio, whether it is homozygous or heterozygous.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mutation is best described as
options: the normal process of gamete formation
the transfer of pollen between flowers
a sudden, random change in the genetic material (DNA) of an organism
the blending of parental traits in offspring
questions.explanation: Mutations are spontaneous or induced changes in DNA sequence that can alter genes or chromosomes, serving as an important source of new genetic variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: An ecosystem is best defined as
options: a community of living organisms interacting with each other and their non-living environment
a single population of one species
a group of organisms of the same species living together
the non-living components of the environment only
questions.explanation: An ecosystem encompasses both the biotic community (living organisms) and the abiotic (non-living) environment, together with the interactions between them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Organisms that manufacture their own organic food from inorganic substances, such as green plants, are called
questions.explanation: Producers (autotrophs), mainly green plants and algae, form the base of most food chains by converting light energy into chemical energy via photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Organisms that feed directly on producers are termed
questions.explanation: Primary consumers, or herbivores, occupy the second trophic level, feeding directly on plant material produced by producers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, play a vital ecological role by
options: converting nitrogen gas directly into protein
breaking down dead organic matter and releasing nutrients back into the environment
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients locked in dead organisms and waste by breaking them down into simpler inorganic substances usable by producers again.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A food web differs from a simple food chain in that a food web
options: has energy flowing in a single, unbranched line
shows the many interconnected feeding relationships within a community
questions.explanation: A food web is a more realistic representation than a single food chain, showing multiple interconnected feeding pathways among many different organisms in a community.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The main process by which atmospheric nitrogen gas is converted into a usable form (nitrates) for plants, carried out by certain soil bacteria, is called
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as Rhizobium in root nodules, convert inert atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia and nitrogenous compounds usable by plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In the carbon cycle, carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere mainly through
questions.explanation: Both the respiration of living organisms and the combustion of fuels (including fossil fuels) release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere, balancing its removal by photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A biome characterised by low rainfall, extreme temperature ranges, and sparse vegetation adapted to conserve water is the
questions.explanation: Deserts receive very little rainfall and experience large daily temperature swings, so their vegetation (e.g., cacti) shows strong adaptations for water conservation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The tropical rainforest biome is characterised mainly by
options: extreme cold with very short growing seasons
high rainfall, warm temperatures, and very high biodiversity
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests receive abundant rainfall year-round and warm, stable temperatures, supporting some of the highest levels of biodiversity on Earth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a density-dependent factor limiting population growth?
options: An unusually cold winter affecting all individuals equally
Competition for food among members of the population
A flood destroying habitat regardless of population size
questions.explanation: Density-dependent factors, like competition, disease spread, and predation, have effects that intensify as population density increases, unlike density-independent factors like natural disasters.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which human activity is a major contributor to environmental pollution through the release of excess carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases?
questions.explanation: Burning coal, petroleum, and natural gas releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and other pollutants, driving climate change and air pollution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Overgrazing and deforestation commonly lead to which environmental problem?
options: Higher rainfall in the affected area
questions.explanation: Removing vegetation cover through overgrazing or deforestation exposes soil to wind and water erosion, often leading to long-term land degradation and desertification.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'conservation' in an ecological context?
options: The uncontrolled extraction of natural resources for economic gain
The process of converting forests into farmland
The careful management and sustainable use of natural resources to prevent their depletion
The complete prohibition of any use of natural resources
questions.explanation: Conservation involves the wise, sustainable management of resources such as forests, wildlife, and water to ensure their availability for future generations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A population, in ecological terms, refers to
options: a single organism and its immediate offspring
the physical habitat of an organism
all the different species living in an area
all the individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a given time
questions.explanation: A population consists of interbreeding individuals of one species occupying a defined geographic area during a specific period.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which ecological factor is classified as a biotic (living) factor rather than an abiotic factor?
questions.explanation: Biotic factors involve interactions with other living organisms (predation, competition, disease), while abiotic factors are non-living physical/chemical conditions like temperature and rainfall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The theory of evolution proposes that
options: all species were created independently and remain unchanged
species never change over geological time
present-day species have descended, with gradual modification, from earlier, often simpler ancestral forms
organisms can acquire entirely new organs within a single generation by will
questions.explanation: Evolutionary theory holds that all life shares common ancestry, with species gradually changing over long time periods through processes such as natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Lamarck's theory of evolution proposed that
options: evolution occurs suddenly within a single generation
natural selection acts on random genetic variation
species arise only through special creation
acquired characteristics developed during an organism's lifetime could be inherited by its offspring
questions.explanation: Lamarck's theory of 'inheritance of acquired characteristics' (e.g., a giraffe's neck lengthening from stretching, then being passed to offspring) is now considered incorrect by modern genetics.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution is primarily based on the mechanism of
options: natural selection acting on heritable variation
questions.explanation: Darwin proposed that individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully, gradually shifting a population's characteristics over generations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered strong evidence for evolution from comparative anatomy?
options: The presence of water in all living cells
Homologous structures, such as the similar bone arrangement in a bird's wing and a human arm
The universal use of the same language of instruction in biology
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share a similar underlying skeletal arrangement despite different functions, suggesting descent from a common ancestor, a key evolutionary evidence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Fossils provide evidence for evolution mainly by
options: proving that all species appeared at the same time
showing a chronological record of gradual changes in organisms over geological time
demonstrating spontaneous generation of new species
questions.explanation: The fossil record, when arranged by the age of rock strata, often shows a progressive sequence of gradual anatomical change, supporting the concept of evolution over time.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Vestigial structures, such as the human appendix, are considered evidence for evolution because they
options: prove that acquired characteristics are inherited
are remnants of organs that were functional in ancestral species but have reduced or lost function today
appear only in the fossil record, never in living organisms
questions.explanation: Vestigial organs are reduced, seemingly non-functional structures inherited from ancestors in whom they served a clear purpose, suggesting evolutionary descent with modification.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Natural selection acts on variation within a population mainly through differences in
options: survival and reproductive success among individuals with different heritable traits
the total number of offspring produced regardless of trait
the age at which individuals die of natural causes only
random mutation rates that are identical for all individuals
questions.explanation: Individuals with traits better suited to their environment tend to survive longer and produce more offspring, passing those advantageous traits on more frequently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Adaptation, in the context of evolution, refers to
options: the process of an individual organism changing its own body structure at will
a heritable trait that improves an organism's chances of survival and reproduction in its environment
a trait that has no effect on survival
any random change acquired during an organism's life
questions.explanation: Adaptations are inherited features shaped by natural selection over generations that enhance an organism's fitness for its specific environment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of camouflage as an adaptation for survival?
options: A fish having gills for respiration
A chameleon changing colour to blend with its surroundings
A cactus storing water in its stem
questions.explanation: Camouflage allows organisms to blend with their environment, reducing detection by predators or improving success as a predator, a classic survival adaptation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The concept of 'survival of the fittest' in evolutionary theory means that
options: all organisms in a population have an equal chance of survival regardless of traits
organisms best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce
only the physically strongest organisms in a population ever survive
fitness refers only to physical strength and speed
questions.explanation: 'Fitness' in evolutionary biology means reproductive success relative to the environment, not just physical strength, so well-adapted individuals of any trait can be 'fittest'.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Members of the kingdom Protista are mainly characterised by being
options: eukaryotic and mostly unicellular organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium
prokaryotic organisms lacking a true nucleus
organisms that reproduce only by spore formation on land
multicellular organisms with differentiated tissues and organs
questions.explanation: Protists are eukaryotic organisms, mostly unicellular, that do not fit neatly into the plant, animal, or fungal kingdoms, such as Amoeba and Paramecium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of the kingdom Animalia?
options: Prokaryotic organisms with no membrane-bound organelles
Organisms with cell walls made of chitin that absorb their food
Organisms that photosynthesise using chlorophyll in chloroplasts
Multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic organisms that typically lack cell walls
questions.explanation: Animals are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls that obtain nutrition heterotrophically by ingesting other organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Members of the kingdom Plantae are distinguished from animals mainly by
options: obtaining nutrients only by absorbing dead organic matter
having cellulose cell walls and chlorophyll for photosynthesis
lacking any form of cell wall
questions.explanation: Plants possess cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll, enabling them to manufacture their own food through photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Viruses are generally excluded from the five-kingdom classification system because they
options: are non-cellular and can only reproduce inside a living host cell
are prokaryotic organisms similar to bacteria
questions.explanation: Viruses lack cellular structure and independent metabolism, replicating only by hijacking the machinery of a living host cell, so they fall outside the five kingdoms of living organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The five-kingdom system of classification (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) was proposed by
questions.explanation: Robert Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification system in 1969, grouping organisms based on cell structure, nutrition, and organisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which class of vertebrates is characterised by moist, scaleless skin and a life cycle that typically begins with an aquatic, gill-breathing larval stage?
questions.explanation: Amphibians such as frogs typically hatch as aquatic, gill-breathing tadpoles before metamorphosing into air-breathing adults with moist, permeable skin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A major distinguishing feature of the phylum Arthropoda is
options: a soft, unsegmented body protected by a calcareous shell
a segmented body with jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton
the presence of a backbone enclosing the spinal cord
the absence of any body segmentation
questions.explanation: Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids) are defined by segmented bodies, paired jointed appendages, and a hard exoskeleton made of chitin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The cell theory, which states that all living organisms are composed of cells, is credited mainly to the work of
questions.explanation: Matthias Schleiden (plants) and Theodor Schwann (animals) jointly proposed that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in all living organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The Golgi apparatus in a cell functions mainly to
options: synthesise proteins directly from messenger RNA
modify, package, and sort proteins for secretion or use within the cell
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them, and packages them into vesicles for secretion or delivery to other organelles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, is mainly involved in
options: the digestion of worn-out cell parts
the storage of lipids and steroids
the generation of ATP through respiration
the synthesis and transport of proteins within the cell
questions.explanation: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesise proteins, which are then folded and transported through its membranous channels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Lysosomes within a cell function mainly to
options: contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and cellular debris
direct all hereditary activities of the cell
store water and maintain turgor pressure
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest damaged organelles, foreign material, and cellular waste.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The large central vacuole found in a mature plant cell mainly functions to
options: house the chromosomes during cell division
maintain turgor pressure by storing water and dissolved solutes
questions.explanation: The central vacuole stores water and solutes, and the resulting osmotic pressure pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall, keeping the cell turgid and rigid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The plant cell wall is composed mainly of
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls consist mainly of cellulose fibres, which give the wall its characteristic strength while remaining freely permeable to water and solutes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A key structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells is that prokaryotic cells
options: are always larger than eukaryotic cells
lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
possess a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, lack a nucleus enclosed in a membrane and lack membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria, unlike eukaryotic cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: During the prophase stage of mitosis, the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and
options: the chromosomes align at the cell's equator
sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
the nuclear membrane begins to break down as spindle fibres start to form
the cell membrane pinches inward to divide the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: In prophase, chromatin condenses into distinct chromosomes, the nuclear envelope disintegrates, and spindle fibres begin to form in preparation for chromosome alignment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Meiosis contributes to genetic variation in offspring mainly through
options: crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes
the formation of two identical diploid daughter cells
the fusion of two gametes during fertilisation
the exact duplication of chromosomes before division
questions.explanation: During meiosis, crossing over between homologous chromosomes and their independent assortment shuffle genetic material, producing gametes with new combinations of alleles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The centromere of a chromosome is best described as the region that
options: is found only in prokaryotic cells
contains the genes coding for ribosomal proteins only
joins sister chromatids together and serves as the attachment point for spindle fibres
questions.explanation: The centromere is the constricted region holding sister chromatids together, and spindle fibres attach here to pull chromatids apart during cell division.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The reduction of leaves to spines in cactus plants is a structural adaptation that mainly helps to
options: increase the rate of photosynthesis in the leaves
increase the surface area for gaseous exchange
reduce water loss through transpiration in a dry environment
questions.explanation: By reducing leaves to spines, cacti minimise the surface area exposed to the dry desert air, greatly reducing water loss through transpiration, while photosynthesis occurs in the fleshy stem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The ability of the camel's kidney to produce a small volume of highly concentrated urine is an example of a
options: structural adaptation for locomotion on sand
physiological adaptation for water conservation in a desert environment
questions.explanation: Producing highly concentrated urine is an internal, functional (physiological) adaptation that allows the camel to conserve body water in its arid habitat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The seasonal, long-distance movement of certain birds to warmer regions in search of food and favourable breeding conditions is an example of
options: a physiological adaptation for temperature regulation
a behavioural adaptation known as migration
questions.explanation: Migration is a learned or instinctive behavioural adaptation that allows animals to avoid unfavourable seasonal conditions by moving to more suitable habitats.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Stomata on the surface of a leaf mainly function to allow
options: the exchange of gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen with the atmosphere
the transport of manufactured food to the roots
the absorption of water and mineral salts from the soil
the anchorage of the plant to the substrate
questions.explanation: Stomata are microscopic pores in the leaf epidermis that permit carbon dioxide to enter for photosynthesis and allow oxygen and water vapour to exit.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Nitrogen is an essential mineral element for plants mainly because it is required for the synthesis of
options: calcium pectate for the middle lamella
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is a key component of amino acids (and thus proteins) and of the chlorophyll molecule, so a deficiency severely limits plant growth and causes yellowing of leaves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A plant showing chlorosis, or yellowing of the leaves, due to reduced chlorophyll production is most likely deficient in the mineral
questions.explanation: Magnesium is a central component of the chlorophyll molecule, so its deficiency impairs chlorophyll synthesis, resulting in yellowing (chlorosis) of leaves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, aids digestion mainly by
options: emulsifying fats into smaller droplets to increase the surface area for enzyme action
neutralising excess acid in the large intestine
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area available for lipase to act upon during fat digestion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The pancreas contributes to digestion mainly by secreting pancreatic juice containing
options: amylase, lipase, and trypsin into the small intestine
questions.explanation: The pancreas secretes a mixture of digestive enzymes, including amylase, lipase, and trypsin, into the duodenum to digest carbohydrates, fats, and proteins respectively.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The finger-like projections lining the small intestine, called villi, function mainly to
options: secrete hydrochloric acid for protein digestion
increase the surface area available for the absorption of digested food
questions.explanation: Villi greatly increase the internal surface area of the small intestine, each containing a network of capillaries and a lacteal that efficiently absorb digested nutrients.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A major function of the large intestine (colon) in the digestive system is to
options: absorb the bulk of digested nutrients into the blood
carry out the initial digestion of starch
absorb water and some salts from undigested food, forming faeces
questions.explanation: The large intestine reabsorbs water and some mineral salts from the indigestible food residue, compacting it into semi-solid faeces for elimination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The mammalian molar teeth, with their broad, ridged surfaces, are mainly adapted for
options: grinding and crushing food before swallowing
questions.explanation: Molars have broad, flattened, ridged crowns that efficiently grind and crush food, especially plant material, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Carnivorous mammals typically possess specialised carnassial teeth, which are adapted for
options: shearing and slicing through flesh and tendons
questions.explanation: Carnassial teeth are modified premolars and molars with sharp, blade-like edges that shear through meat and tendons efficiently, an adaptation for a carnivorous diet.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The mammalian heart is divided internally into how many chambers?
questions.explanation: The mammalian heart has four chambers, two upper atria that receive blood and two lower, more muscular ventricles that pump blood out of the heart.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A major advantage of the double circulatory system found in mammals is that it
options: reduces the total number of heart chambers required
allows blood to pass through the heart twice per full circuit, maintaining higher blood pressure and more efficient oxygen delivery
eliminates the need for a closed circulatory system
allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix freely
questions.explanation: In double circulation, blood returns to the heart after passing through the lungs before being pumped again to the body, keeping pressure high and preventing dilution of oxygenated blood.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: White blood cells (leucocytes) in the blood mainly function to
options: defend the body against infection through phagocytosis and antibody production
transport digested food from the gut
initiate blood clotting at a wound site
questions.explanation: White blood cells are part of the immune system, engulfing pathogens by phagocytosis or producing antibodies to fight infection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Platelets present in mammalian blood are essential mainly for
options: initiating the process of blood clotting at a wound
questions.explanation: Platelets release substances that trigger a cascade of reactions converting fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a clot that seals wounds and prevents blood loss.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Transpiration in plants is best defined as the
options: upward movement of water in the xylem vessels
loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata
process of photosynthesis occurring in the leaf
uptake of water by root hairs from the soil
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour from plant surfaces, chiefly through open stomata in the leaves, which also helps draw water up through the xylem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Guard cells surrounding a stoma regulate its opening and closing mainly by
options: absorbing carbon dioxide directly from the air
secreting enzymes that digest the stomatal pore
changing their turgidity in response to water content and light conditions
questions.explanation: When guard cells become turgid (usually in light, with adequate water), they bow outward and open the stoma; when they lose turgor, the stoma closes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The alveoli of the human lungs are well adapted for efficient gaseous exchange mainly because they are
options: thick-walled and lined with cartilage rings
connected directly to the heart's ventricles
surrounded by skeletal muscle for contraction
thin-walled, moist, and richly supplied with blood capillaries, providing a large surface area
questions.explanation: Alveoli have very thin, moist walls, a vast total surface area, and a dense network of capillaries, all of which maximise the rate of diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: During inhalation in humans, the diaphragm
options: remains completely still while the ribs do all the work
contracts to force air out of the lungs
relaxes and domes upward, decreasing thoracic volume
contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction flattens its dome shape, enlarging the thoracic cavity and lowering internal pressure, causing air to be drawn into the lungs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: When yeast respires anaerobically in the absence of oxygen, the glucose is broken down to produce
options: lactic acid and a large amount of energy
ethanol, carbon dioxide, and a small amount of energy
water, carbon dioxide, and a large amount of energy
questions.explanation: Yeast carries out alcoholic fermentation, converting glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide while releasing only a small amount of usable energy, a process exploited in brewing and baking.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Deamination, a process carried out in the liver, involves the
options: conversion of glucose into fat for storage
synthesis of bile salts from cholesterol
removal of the amino group from excess amino acids to form urea
questions.explanation: During deamination, the liver removes the nitrogen-containing amino group from surplus amino acids, converting it into urea for excretion by the kidneys.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of the human skeletal system?
options: Enabling movement in conjunction with muscles
questions.explanation: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, and works with muscles to enable movement, but it does not manufacture digestive enzymes, a function of glands like the pancreas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In the human arm, the biceps and triceps muscles work as an antagonistic pair, meaning that
options: the triceps alone is responsible for all arm movement
the biceps contracts to flex the arm while the triceps contracts to extend it
both muscles always contract together to move the arm
the biceps and triceps never act on the same joint
questions.explanation: Antagonistic muscle pairs work in opposition; the biceps contracts to bend (flex) the elbow while the triceps contracts to straighten (extend) it, since muscles can only pull, not push.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The structure that attaches a skeletal muscle to a bone, transmitting the force of contraction, is called a
questions.explanation: Tendons are tough, fibrous connective tissue that anchor muscles to bones, whereas ligaments connect bone to bone at joints.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Seeds such as those of the dandelion, which possess a feathery parachute-like structure, are adapted for dispersal by
questions.explanation: Light seeds with feathery or winged structures are carried easily by air currents over long distances, an adaptation for wind dispersal.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is generally required for the germination of a typical seed?
options: Adequate water, oxygen, and a suitable temperature
High salt concentration and no oxygen
questions.explanation: Seeds require water to activate enzymes, oxygen for aerobic respiration, and a suitable temperature for metabolic activity to begin germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The primary functions of the testes in the human male reproductive system are to
options: produce sperm cells and secrete the hormone testosterone
questions.explanation: The testes contain seminiferous tubules that produce sperm through spermatogenesis, and interstitial cells that secrete testosterone, the male sex hormone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In complete metamorphosis, as seen in butterflies, the insect develops through the stages of
options: egg and adult only, with no intermediate stages
questions.explanation: Complete metamorphosis involves four distinct stages, egg, larva, pupa, and adult, with the larva and adult often looking and feeding very differently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The plant hormone primarily responsible for cell elongation and the bending of a shoot towards a light source (phototropism) is
questions.explanation: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side of a shoot, stimulating greater cell elongation there and causing the shoot to bend towards the light.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In flowering plants, active cell division responsible for growth occurs mainly in regions called
questions.explanation: Meristematic tissue, located at root and shoot tips (apical meristems) and in the cambium, consists of continually dividing, undifferentiated cells responsible for plant growth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A reflex action, such as quickly withdrawing a hand from a hot object, is best described as a
options: rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought
hormonal response mediated by the endocrine system
response that only occurs during sleep
slow, voluntary response controlled by the cerebrum
questions.explanation: Reflex actions are fast, automatic, protective responses coordinated by the spinal cord via a reflex arc, bypassing the need for conscious processing in the brain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The hormone adrenaline, secreted by the adrenal medulla in response to stress or danger, prepares the body for 'fight or flight' mainly by
options: regulating water reabsorption in the kidney
lowering blood pressure and heart rate
increasing heart rate and blood glucose levels for rapid energy release
questions.explanation: Adrenaline rapidly increases heart rate, dilates airways, and raises blood glucose levels, mobilising the body's resources for an immediate physical response to danger.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: An organism occupying the top of a food chain, feeding on secondary consumers, is called a
questions.explanation: Tertiary consumers are carnivores that feed on secondary consumers, typically occupying the highest trophic level in a food chain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a pyramid of energy, the amount of energy available generally decreases at each successive trophic level mainly because
options: energy is created anew at each trophic level
consumers absorb 100% of the energy from the level below
producers trap more energy than they use
much energy is lost as heat during respiration at each level
questions.explanation: At each trophic level, a large proportion of the energy consumed is lost as heat through respiration and in undigested waste, so only a small fraction is passed on to the next level.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The overall direction of energy flow through an ecosystem's food chains is best described as
options: unidirectional, moving from producers to various levels of consumers
cyclical, returning fully back to producers
questions.explanation: Unlike nutrients, which are recycled, energy flows in one direction only through an ecosystem, entering as sunlight and being progressively lost as heat at each trophic transfer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The association between a fungus and an alga living together as a lichen, in which both partners benefit, is an example of
questions.explanation: In a lichen, the fungus provides structure and water absorption while the alga (or cyanobacterium) provides food via photosynthesis, so both partners benefit in this mutualistic relationship.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A relationship in which one organism benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed is termed
questions.explanation: Commensalism describes a relationship where one species gains a benefit, such as shelter or transport, while the other species experiences no significant effect.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Competition occurring between individuals of the same species for a limited resource, such as food or mates, is called
questions.explanation: Intraspecific competition occurs among members of the same species, whereas interspecific competition occurs between individuals of different species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The 'niche' of an organism, as distinct from its habitat, refers to
options: the total population size of the species
the taxonomic classification of the organism
the functional role it plays within its ecosystem, including its feeding relationships and interactions
only the physical location where the organism lives
questions.explanation: While habitat describes where an organism lives, its ecological niche describes its functional role, including how it obtains food, interacts with other species, and affects its environment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The uppermost layer of a soil profile, typically dark in colour and richest in organic matter and nutrients, is called the
questions.explanation: The topsoil, or A horizon, is the uppermost soil layer, rich in humus and nutrients, and is where most plant roots and soil organisms are concentrated.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Humus, an important component of fertile soil, improves soil quality mainly by
options: preventing root penetration into the soil
increasing water retention and supplying nutrients as it decomposes
reducing the number of soil microorganisms
questions.explanation: Humus, derived from decomposed organic matter, improves soil structure, boosts water-holding capacity, and gradually releases nutrients as it continues to break down.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In the water cycle, the loss of water vapour from plant leaves into the atmosphere is specifically termed
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the specific term for water vapour loss from plant surfaces, contributing significantly to atmospheric moisture alongside evaporation from open water bodies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Excessive use of chemical fertilisers that run off into rivers and lakes commonly leads to eutrophication, a process in which
options: soil fertility in the surrounding farmland increases dramatically
excess nutrients cause algal blooms that deplete dissolved oxygen, killing aquatic life
questions.explanation: Eutrophication occurs when nutrient-rich runoff triggers excessive algal growth; as the algae die and decompose, oxygen-consuming bacteria deplete dissolved oxygen, causing fish kills.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Acid rain is mainly caused by the release of which gases from the burning of fossil fuels?
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides released from burning fossil fuels react with atmospheric water vapour to form sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as acid rain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The 'greenhouse effect', linked to global warming, refers to the
options: cooling of the Earth's surface due to reflected sunlight
formation of acid rain from industrial gases
trapping of heat in the atmosphere by gases such as carbon dioxide and methane
depletion of the ozone layer by chlorofluorocarbons
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane absorb and re-radiate infrared heat, trapping it within the Earth's atmosphere and gradually raising global temperatures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Large-scale deforestation can contribute to climate change mainly because it
options: has no measurable effect on the carbon cycle
reduces the removal of atmospheric carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, increasing greenhouse gas levels
increases the amount of oxygen released by plants
questions.explanation: Fewer trees mean less carbon dioxide is absorbed through photosynthesis, while the burning or decay of felled trees releases stored carbon, both increasing atmospheric CO2 levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The maximum population size that a given environment can sustainably support, considering available resources, is known as the
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the largest population size an environment can support indefinitely given the food, water, space, and other resources available.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a classic predator-prey relationship, such as between the lynx and the snowshoe hare, population sizes typically
options: fluctuate cyclically, with predator numbers rising and falling in response to prey abundance
remain constant and unaffected by each other
questions.explanation: Predator and prey populations commonly show linked cyclical fluctuations, as an increase in prey supports more predators, whose increased predation later reduces the prey population.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The quadrat method used by ecologists is mainly employed to
options: measure rainfall and temperature in an ecosystem
determine the genetic makeup of a population
measure the exact age of individual organisms
estimate the population density and distribution of organisms within a habitat
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a sampling frame placed at random or systematic points within a habitat to count organisms, allowing ecologists to estimate overall population density and distribution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Ecological succession refers to the
options: annual migration pattern of a species
gradual, predictable change in the species composition of a community over time
sudden and permanent destruction of an ecosystem
process by which a single species evolves into another
questions.explanation: Ecological succession describes the orderly progression of community changes over time, from pioneer species colonising bare ground to an eventual, relatively stable climax community.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Solar energy, wind, and forest timber are generally classified as
questions.explanation: Renewable resources are naturally replenished within a human lifetime, unlike non-renewable resources such as coal, oil, and natural gas, which take millions of years to form.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Conservation efforts aimed at protecting endangered species are important mainly because they help to
options: increase the population of predators uncontrollably
maintain biodiversity and prevent the permanent loss of species from an ecosystem
questions.explanation: Protecting endangered species preserves genetic diversity and the ecological roles those species play, helping to maintain the overall stability and functioning of ecosystems.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Every cell in a normal human body (except gametes) contains how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Normal human somatic cells are diploid, containing 46 chromosomes organised into 23 homologous pairs, one set inherited from each parent.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, the sex of an offspring is determined by the combination of sex chromosomes such that
options: XX and XY both always produce females
XX produces a female and XY produces a male
XX produces a male and XY produces a female
the sex is determined solely by the mother's chromosomes
questions.explanation: Females normally carry two X chromosomes (XX) while males carry one X and one Y chromosome (XY); the sperm, carrying either an X or Y, determines the offspring's sex.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that
options: only one allele for a trait exists in a population
genes located on the same chromosome always assort independently
alleles always blend to produce intermediate offspring
genes for different traits are inherited independently of one another during gamete formation
questions.explanation: The law of independent assortment states that allele pairs for different traits separate independently during meiosis, provided the genes are on different chromosomes (or far apart on the same one).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: When a red-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant and all offspring are pink, this is an example of
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote displays an intermediate phenotype, such as pink flowers resulting from a red and white cross.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The AB blood group in humans, in which both the A and B antigens are simultaneously expressed on red blood cells, is an example of
questions.explanation: Codominance occurs when both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed in the phenotype, as seen with the IA and IB alleles both being expressed in the AB blood group.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mendel's law of segregation states that
options: all offspring of a cross will show an identical phenotype
alleles from both parents blend permanently in the offspring
only dominant alleles are passed on to offspring
the two alleles for a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele
questions.explanation: The law of segregation states that during meiosis, the paired alleles for a gene separate so that each gamete receives only one allele from each pair, restoring the pair upon fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a dihybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (e.g., RrYy x RrYy), the expected phenotypic ratio of offspring in the F2 generation is
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross between two heterozygotes for independently assorting genes produces a characteristic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the offspring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Human fingerprint patterns are often cited as an example of variation because they
options: are entirely determined by environmental factors alone
change significantly with a person's age
are identical among all members of a family
are unique to each individual, even among identical twins
questions.explanation: Fingerprint patterns are formed by a complex interaction of genetic and environmental (developmental) factors in the womb, making them unique to each individual, even genetically identical twins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is a major source of genetic variation among offspring of sexually reproducing organisms?
options: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis, and random fertilisation
Binary fission in the parent organism
Mitotic cell division in body tissues
questions.explanation: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis, combined with the random fusion of gametes at fertilisation, generate new combinations of alleles, driving genetic variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Genes that are located close together on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together, rather than assorting independently, are said to show
questions.explanation: Linked genes lie close together on the same chromosome and are usually inherited together as a unit, since they are less likely to be separated by crossing over.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The ABO blood group system in humans, controlled by three possible alleles (IA, IB, and i) at a single gene locus, is an example of
questions.explanation: Multiple allelism refers to a gene having more than two alleles in the population, as seen with the three alleles (IA, IB, i) controlling the ABO blood group system.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Down syndrome in humans is caused by a chromosomal abnormality in which an individual has
questions.explanation: Down syndrome results from nondisjunction during gamete formation, leading to an individual having three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the usual two.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A pedigree chart in genetics is used mainly to
options: measure the exact number of chromosomes in a cell
trace the inheritance pattern of a particular trait through several generations of a family
determine the rate of mutation in a population
calculate the carrying capacity of a habitat
questions.explanation: A pedigree chart records the occurrence of a trait or disorder across generations of a family, helping geneticists determine whether it is dominant, recessive, or sex-linked.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in a human cell, how many pairs are autosomes (non-sex chromosomes)?
questions.explanation: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes, which carry most of the genetic information, plus one additional pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY) that determines sex.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Haemophilia, a blood clotting disorder, is inherited in humans as a
options: sex-linked recessive condition carried on the X chromosome
condition carried only on the Y chromosome
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele located on the X chromosome, explaining why the disorder occurs far more frequently in males than in females.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Human skin colour, which shows a smooth range of shades rather than distinct categories, is best described as an example of
options: polygenic (continuous) inheritance, influenced by several genes
inheritance controlled by a single gene with two alleles
questions.explanation: Skin colour is controlled by several genes acting together (polygenic inheritance), producing a continuous range of phenotypes rather than a few distinct categories.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The peppered moth (Biston betularia), which shifted from predominantly light-coloured to predominantly dark-coloured forms in polluted, industrial areas of England, is a classic example of
options: natural selection acting on existing variation (industrial melanism)
questions.explanation: Dark moths, better camouflaged against soot-blackened tree trunks, survived predation more successfully than light moths in polluted areas, illustrating natural selection favouring an existing variant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The rapid spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is considered strong modern evidence for evolution because it demonstrates
options: spontaneous generation of new bacterial species
that all bacteria are naturally immune to antibiotics
natural selection favouring individuals with a heritable resistance trait when exposed to a selective pressure
the inheritance of characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime
questions.explanation: When exposed to antibiotics, only bacteria with pre-existing resistance genes survive and reproduce, rapidly increasing the frequency of resistance in the population, a direct observation of natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Analogous structures, such as the wings of an insect and the wings of a bird, differ from homologous structures in that they
options: are always found only in closely related species
never appear in unrelated groups of organisms
have the same underlying bone structure inherited from a common ancestor
perform a similar function but arose independently, without a shared evolutionary origin
questions.explanation: Analogous structures perform similar functions due to similar environmental pressures (convergent evolution) but do not share a common evolutionary origin, unlike homologous structures.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Speciation is best defined as the process by which
options: an individual organism adapts to its environment within its own lifetime
two different species interbreed to form a hybrid
a population's chromosome number is halved during meiosis
a new, distinct species arises from an existing ancestral population
questions.explanation: Speciation occurs when populations of the same species diverge, usually through prolonged reproductive isolation, until they can no longer interbreed and are considered separate species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: When a physical barrier, such as a mountain range or river, separates a population into two groups that evolve independently, this can eventually lead to
options: identical evolutionary changes in both groups
increased gene flow between the groups
a return to a single interbreeding population
questions.explanation: Geographic isolation prevents gene flow between separated populations, allowing them to accumulate different mutations and adaptations independently, potentially resulting in the formation of new species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The striking similarities observed in the early embryonic stages of fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals (comparative embryology) are considered evidence for
options: the concept of vestigial organs only
a shared evolutionary ancestry among vertebrates
questions.explanation: Vertebrate embryos show remarkably similar early developmental features (such as gill slits and tails), suggesting that these groups share a common evolutionary ancestor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Darwin observed that organisms typically produce far more offspring than can survive to reproduce, leading to a 'struggle for existence.' This observation was influenced by the writings of
options: Thomas Malthus on population growth and limited resources
questions.explanation: Darwin drew on Thomas Malthus's essay on population, which argued that populations grow faster than food supply, to develop the idea that limited resources drive competition and natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Darwin's observations of finches with different beak shapes adapted to different food sources on the Galapagos Islands, made during the voyage of HMS Beagle, provided important support for his theory of
questions.explanation: The varying beak shapes of Galapagos finches, each suited to a different food source, illustrated how populations can diverge and adapt to different niches, a key observation supporting natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Archaeopteryx, a fossil possessing both reptilian features (teeth, a bony tail) and avian features (feathers, wings), is significant to evolutionary biology as an example of a
options: transitional fossil linking reptiles and birds
vestigial organism with no evolutionary significance
purely reptilian organism with no bird traits
questions.explanation: Archaeopteryx displays a mixture of reptilian and avian characteristics, making it a classic transitional fossil that supports the evolutionary link between dinosaurs/reptiles and modern birds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The observation that marsupial mammals (such as kangaroos) are found predominantly in Australia, isolated from placental mammals elsewhere, is used as evidence for evolution from the field of
options: biogeography, the study of species distribution across geography
questions.explanation: Biogeography shows that unique groups of organisms, like Australia's marsupials, evolved in geographic isolation, supporting the idea that species diverge independently once separated from related populations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Dolphins (mammals) and sharks (fish) both have similarly streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies suited to fast swimming, despite not sharing a recent common ancestor. This is an example of
options: homologous structures inherited from a common ancestor
convergent evolution, where unrelated species evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures
divergent evolution from a shared ancestor
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar adaptations because they face similar environmental pressures, such as the need for a streamlined body for efficient swimming.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mutations are considered important in the process of evolution mainly because they
options: introduce new heritable variation into a population upon which natural selection can act
occur identically and simultaneously in every member of a population
always improve the fitness of the organism that carries them
are inherited only if acquired during the parent's lifetime
questions.explanation: Mutations are the ultimate source of new alleles in a population; while most are neutral or harmful, occasionally a mutation proves advantageous and can be favoured by natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Comparative studies of DNA and protein sequences across different species provide evidence for evolution mainly by showing that
options: DNA sequences cannot be compared between different species
all species have identical DNA sequences
protein sequences never change over evolutionary time
species with more similar sequences are generally more closely related through common ancestry
questions.explanation: The degree of similarity in DNA and protein sequences between species generally reflects how recently they shared a common ancestor, providing strong molecular evidence for evolutionary relationships.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Bacteria belonging to the kingdom Monera reproduce mainly by
options: spore formation within a fruiting body only
binary fission, a rapid form of asexual reproduction
budding from a parent cell over several weeks
complex sexual reproduction involving distinct male and female gametes
questions.explanation: Most bacteria reproduce asexually and rapidly through binary fission, in which a single cell duplicates its DNA and divides into two genetically identical daughter cells.
